title: Skills Inside Subagents — the genuinely confusing case

questions.prompt: Your API subagent ignores a team conventions skill. You want that skill's content present before it starts writing code. Which change does it?
options: Add skills: [api-conventions] to the subagent's frontmatter
Add context: fork to the conventions skill's frontmatter
Move the conventions into CLAUDE.md
Add the skill name to the delegation message each time you ask
questions.explanation: The `skills` field preloads full skill content into the subagent's context at startup, so the knowledge is there before work begins. Option B forks the skill into a fresh subagent where those guidelines become a prompt with no task — the classic empty result. Option C puts it in the subagent's window but nowhere near the endpoint code being written. Option D works but re-pays every run and depends on you remembering.

questions.prompt: A subagent lists skills: [deploy-conventions] in its frontmatter. You want it to be unable to invoke any skill at all, including ones you didn't list. What actually enforces that?
options: skills: — listing one skill already makes it the only reachable one
Remove Skill from the subagent's tools, or add it to disallowedTools
set disable-model-invocation: true on every other skill in the repo
Nothing — subagents can't invoke skills, only preload them
questions.explanation: `skills` selects what's preloaded, not what's reachable — a subagent can still invoke project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool during the run. Removing Skill from the allowlist or denying it is the enforcement layer. Option C is both global and backwards: it would break your own invocations, and it's the wrong tool for scoping one agent. Option D is false — subagents can invoke skills.

questions.prompt: A skill whose body is only "use these API conventions" is set to context: fork. Running it returns something vague or empty. Why?
options: The skills field was missing so the content never loaded
forked skills need a model field or they default to refusing work
context: fork makes the skill the subagent's prompt, and a guideline with no task gives it nothing to do
Explore and Plan can't run skills and the default agent was Plan
questions.explanation: context: fork turns the rendered SKILL.md into the subagent's prompt, so a skill needs explicit instructions with a task — a bare guideline leaves the subagent with principles and no work, and it returns without meaningful output. Option A confuses the two directions; the `skills` field belongs on the subagent, not the skill. Option D misreads which agent type applies — the default is general-purpose, and none of the listed agents are the cause.

questions.prompt: A forked skill edits three files in the background. You run /rewind expecting the edits to be undone and they aren't. Why?
options: /rewind only handles the main conversation, which is exactly this case
The skill's context: fork field wasn't committed to version control
A backgrounded fork runs outside the session's checkpoints, so /rewind never reaches its edits
Edits from any subagent are permanent by design
questions.explanation: Backgrounded forks specifically fall outside session checkpoints — that's why the guidance is to revert them with git rather than /rewind. Option A inverts it: /rewind handles the main conversation, and this edit isn't in it. Option C's scope is wrong too — foreground subagent edits do fall under checkpoints; it's the background-fork case that's outside them.

questions.prompt: You want a subagent that has your whole conversation, plus the option to edit files. Which combination is right?
options: A skill with context: fork and an agent field pointing at general-purpose
A fork — /subtask — with isolation: worktree if the edits must not touch your checkout
A custom subagent with skills: preloaded, since preloading carries conversation history
A fresh subagent with omitClaudeMd: false, which inherits the parent conversation
questions.explanation: Only a fork inherits the full parent conversation; /subtask starts one, and isolation: worktree redirects its file edits into a separate worktree so your checkout stays clean. Option A gets the name backwards — context: fork creates a fresh isolated context and does not carry your history. Option B is wrong because preloading skills injects reference text, not conversation. Option D is also wrong: omitting CLAUDE.md controls instruction files, not history.
